text: A nurse assesses a client and finds them increasingly difficult to arouse compared to one hour ago. What is the priority nursing action?

options.B: Notify the provider immediately — LOC is the most sensitive indicator of neuro change
options.D: Reposition the client and recheck in 30 minutes

trapLogic: ATI wants you to recognize that ANY downward trend in LOC is the earliest and most sensitive sign of neuro deterioration — it always outranks 'wait and see' options.

text: Which categories of causes should the nurse consider when a client presents with new altered LOC of unknown origin? (Select all that apply — think AEIOU TIPS)

options.B: Structural
options.C: Purely psychological, rule out all physical causes first

trapLogic: The trap answer says to rule out physical causes 'first' as if psych is separate — ATI wants LOC worked up broadly (metabolic/structural/toxic/infectious) simultaneously, not sequentially dismissing physical causes.

text: A client has a single seizure after a high fever. The nurse understands this client does NOT yet meet the definition of epilepsy because:

options.B: Epilepsy = 2 or more UNPROVOKED seizures; this seizure was provoked (fever)
options.D: One seizure always requires antiepileptic drugs

trapLogic: Trap: students confuse 'seizure' with 'epilepsy.' A provoked, single seizure is not epilepsy — epilepsy needs recurrence AND no clear provoking cause.

text: The nurse is differentiating a vegetative state from a coma. Which finding is consistent with a vegetative state rather than coma?

options.A: Eyes remain closed at all times
options.B: No sleep-wake cycle at all
options.C: Eyes open with sleep-wake cycles present, but no awareness

trapLogic: Trap: 'eyes open' makes students think 'awake/aware.' Vegetative state = eyes OPEN, cycles present, but zero awareness — that combination is the whole trap.

text: A client arrives with ischemic stroke symptoms that began 2 hours ago. Which finding would EXCLUDE the client from receiving tPA?

options.B: BP of 190/115 that cannot be lowered below 185/110

trapLogic: ATI loves testing the exact BP cutoff (<185/110) as an exclusion criterion — a BP just above threshold is the trap distractor.

text: Which order should the nurse question in the first 24 hours after a client receives tPA for ischemic stroke?

options.B: Aspirin 81 mg now

trapLogic: Trap: anticoagulants/antiplatelets are held for 24 hours post-tPA due to bleeding risk — a 'reasonable-sounding' med order is exactly what ATI slips in.

text: Before giving a stroke client their first meal, what must the nurse do first?

options.A: Assist to a full upright position and serve a regular diet
options.B: Perform a swallowing/dysphagia screen
options.C: Administer the client's routine medications with food
options.D: Ask the family to feed the client

trapLogic: Classic sequencing trap — swallow screening must occur BEFORE any oral intake including meds, water, or food, due to aspiration risk.

text: In the acute phase of ischemic stroke (without elevated ICP), what head-of-bed position optimizes cerebral perfusion?

options.B: Flat, 0 degrees only, never elevated

trapLogic: Trap: students think 'flat is always best for perfusion' — the actual range is 0-30°, and this changes if ICP is elevated (then higher HOB is used instead).

text: A client with multiple sclerosis reports that symptoms worsen after a hot shower. The nurse explains this is due to:

options.A: A new relapse requiring IV steroids
options.B: Uhthoff's phenomenon — heat temporarily worsens nerve conduction, it is NOT a true relapse
options.D: Normal disease progression requiring medication change

trapLogic: Trap: students panic and think 'relapse.' Heat-related worsening is Uhthoff's phenomenon — temporary, resolves with cooling, not a true exacerbation.

text: An MS client is having an acute relapse. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate?

options.B: High-dose IV methylprednisolone

trapLogic: Straightforward recall trap disguised with distractors that sound 'supportive care' but aren't the actual first-line relapse treatment.

text: Which client is at HIGHEST risk for peripheral neuropathy with a 'stocking-glove' symptom distribution?

options.B: A client with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
options.D: A client recovering from a broken arm

trapLogic: Diabetes is the #1 cause of peripheral neuropathy — ATI often buries this fact among unrelated but plausible-sounding conditions.

text: A client diagnosed with Bell's palsy is being treated within 72 hours of onset. Which medication class does the nurse expect?

options.B: Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone)

trapLogic: Trap: timing matters — corticosteroids are most effective when started within 72 hours; this detail is often tested directly.

text: What is the PRIORITY nursing intervention for a client with Bell's palsy who cannot fully close one eye?

options.A: Encourage chewing on the affected side
options.B: Apply lubricating eye drops and protect the cornea (e.g., eye patch at night)
options.D: Apply ice to the affected side continuously

trapLogic: Trap: 'chewing on affected side' sounds like a nursing tip but is actually backwards — patients are taught to chew on the UNAFFECTED side. The real priority is corneal protection.

text: A client with myasthenia gravis reports that muscle weakness is worse in the evening than in the morning. The nurse recognizes this as:

options.A: An unrelated new problem requiring immediate workup
options.B: The expected pattern of MG — weakness worsens with activity/as the day progresses, improves with rest
options.C: A sign the client is faking symptoms

trapLogic: Core disease-pattern trap: MG weakness fluctuates with activity/time of day. Missing this leads to over-treating a 'new' problem that is actually classic MG.

text: What is the PRIORITY teaching point for a client newly prescribed pyridostigmine (Mestinon) for myasthenia gravis?

options.A: Take the medication only when symptoms are severe
options.B: Take the medication ON TIME, exactly as scheduled, even if feeling well
options.C: Double the dose if a dose is missed
options.D: Take with an antacid to prevent stomach upset

trapLogic: Timing is everything with Mestinon — a late dose can precipitate a myasthenic crisis. ATI tests strict adherence to schedule, not PRN or 'as needed' framing.

text: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome has ascending weakness now at the level of the mid-thigh. What is the PRIORITY nursing assessment?

options.B: Respiratory status — rate, SpO2, negative inspiratory force

trapLogic: Because paralysis ascends toward the trunk/diaphragm, respiratory failure is the #1 life-threatening complication in GBS — always the priority answer when GBS is ascending.

text: Which finding on CSF analysis is expected in Guillain-Barré syndrome, and which treatment should the nurse question?

options.A: Low protein/high WBC is expected; corticosteroids are first-line
options.B: High protein/normal WBC (albuminocytologic dissociation) is expected; corticosteroids may WORSEN GBS and are avoided
options.C: High protein/high WBC is expected; IVIG is contraindicated
options.D: CSF findings are normal in GBS; antibiotics are first-line

trapLogic: Double trap in one question: (1) know the specific CSF pattern, and (2) know that corticosteroids — normally a 'go-to' for autoimmune disease — are NOT used in GBS.

text: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty rising from the floor by 'walking his hands up his legs' and has calf enlargement. The nurse recognizes these findings as characteristic of:

options.B: Duchenne muscular dystrophy — Gowers' sign and pseudohypertrophy of the calves

trapLogic: Classic pediatric presentation trap — Gowers' sign + calf pseudohypertrophy + young male = Duchenne MD, distinct from the adult autoimmune conditions in the same unit.

text: A client develops sudden difficulty breathing, hives, and facial swelling after a bee sting. What is the FIRST medication the nurse should administer?

options.B: Epinephrine IM

trapLogic: Trap: antihistamines and steroids are supportive, but epinephrine is always the first-line, life-saving drug in true anaphylaxis — a common ATI sequencing trap.

text: A client with hereditary angioedema (HAE) is having a laryngeal swelling episode. Why won't epinephrine relieve this episode?

options.A: HAE is IgE-mediated just like allergic angioedema, so epinephrine should work identically
options.B: HAE is bradykinin-mediated (C1-inhibitor deficiency), not histamine-mediated, so epinephrine has little effect
options.C: The client is allergic to epinephrine
options.D: Epinephrine only works on the skin, not the airway

trapLogic: This is THE classic angioedema trap — students assume all angioedema responds to epi. HAE needs C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant instead.

text: A client taking lisinopril develops lip and tongue swelling with no urticaria. What is the priority action?

options.A: Give epinephrine and continue the lisinopril
options.B: Hold/discontinue the ACE inhibitor and notify the provider; anticipate switching to an ARB
options.D: Reassure the client this is expected and no action is needed

trapLogic: No urticaria + ACE inhibitor use = bradykinin-mediated angioedema trap. The fix is stopping the drug, not treating it like classic allergic angioedema.

text: What is the first-line treatment for seasonal allergic rhinitis?

options.B: Intranasal corticosteroids
options.D: Immunotherapy as the very first step

trapLogic: Trap: antibiotics are a distractor since rhinitis isn't bacterial; immunotherapy is real but not first-line — intranasal steroids are.

text: A client has a BMI of 41. How does the nurse classify this?

options.B: Obese (BMI 30-39.9)

trapLogic: Precise cutoff trap: 30 = obese threshold, 40 = morbid obesity threshold. A BMI of 41 crosses into the second, more severe category.

text: Which waist circumference indicates increased metabolic risk in a male client?

options.B: Greater than 40 inches
options.D: Waist circumference is not a risk indicator

trapLogic: Exact-number recall trap: >40 inches (men) and >35 inches (women) are the metabolic risk thresholds.

text: A client's CD4+ count is 180 cells/mm3. The nurse understands this client:

options.B: Meets the criteria for an AIDS-defining diagnosis (CD4 <200)
options.D: Has an active bacterial infection only

trapLogic: Threshold recall trap: CD4 <200 defines AIDS regardless of symptoms — a value just under 200 is the classic trap number.

text: Which assessment is the PRIORITY in the first few hours after a thyroidectomy?

options.A: Assessing for hemorrhage/swelling and respiratory distress at the surgical site
options.B: Assessing bowel sounds

trapLogic: Airway trumps everything post-thyroidectomy — swelling can rapidly compress the airway, making this the immediate life-threat priority.

text: A post-thyroidectomy client's hand spasms when a blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure. This is a positive:

options.B: Trousseau's sign, indicating hypocalcemia

trapLogic: Sign-matching trap: Chvostek = tapping the facial nerve/cheek; Trousseau = BP cuff-induced carpal spasm. Both indicate hypocalcemia post-thyroidectomy, but the triggers are commonly swapped in test questions.

text: Which type of thyroid cancer carries the WORST prognosis?

options.B: Follicular

trapLogic: Trap: papillary is most common AND has the BEST prognosis — students sometimes assume 'most common' means 'most dangerous.' Anaplastic is rare but most aggressive/worst prognosis.

text: A client with type 1 diabetes presents with fruity breath, Kussmaul respirations, and a glucose of 480. The nurse suspects:

options.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)

trapLogic: DKA hallmark trio: ketones (fruity breath), Kussmaul respirations, and moderately-high (not extreme) glucose — distinct from HHS's much higher glucose with no ketones.

text: A client with type 2 diabetes has a glucose of 950, no ketones, and profound dehydration with altered mental status developing over several days. This presentation is most consistent with:

options.B: HHS

trapLogic: Trap: absence of ketones plus extremely high glucose and SLOW onset over days = HHS, not DKA — students often default to DKA any time glucose is critically elevated.

text: A client reports feeling shaky, sweaty, and confused. Fingerstick glucose is 58. What is the PRIORITY action?

options.B: Give a fast-acting oral carbohydrate (e.g., glucose tablets or juice) if the client can swallow safely
options.C: Call a rapid response and wait for the provider
options.D: Restrict all oral intake until the provider arrives

trapLogic: Classic hypoglycemia trap: giving insulin would worsen a low blood sugar. The priority is fast carbohydrate, not more insulin or delay.

text: When teaching diabetic foot care, which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.A: "I will inspect my feet every day."
options.B: "I will moisturize my feet, including between my toes, every night."

trapLogic: Subtle wording trap: moisturizer should be applied to the feet but NOT between the toes, since trapped moisture there promotes fungal infection and breakdown.

text: How often should a client with poorly controlled diabetes have their A1c checked?

options.B: Every 6 months

trapLogic: Frequency trap: q3 months applies when UNcontrolled; q6 months applies once STABLE. Reading the stem carefully (poorly controlled) determines the correct interval.

text: A nurse disagrees with a plan of care and needs to escalate the concern using a structured communication tool. Which phrase reflects appropriate use of CUS words?

options.A: "I really don't think that's a good idea."
options.B: "I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue."
options.D: "I'll just chart my disagreement and move on."

trapLogic: ATI tests recognition of the exact CUS framework as the professional escalation tool, versus vague or passive alternatives.

text: On percussion, the nurse notes a hyperresonant sound over the client's chest. This finding is most consistent with:

options.B: Pleural effusion

trapLogic: Sound-to-pathology matching trap: hyperresonance = too much air (emphysema/pneumothorax); dullness = fluid or solid tissue (effusion/consolidation) — these are frequently swapped in distractors.

text: Tactile fremitus is INCREASED over an area of the lung. This suggests:

options.B: Pleural effusion

trapLogic: Fremitus increases when sound travels better through solid/consolidated tissue; it decreases with air or fluid in the way (pneumothorax/effusion) — a frequently reversed detail on ATI exams.

text: A client scores high on the STOP-BANG questionnaire. Which finding contributed to this score?

options.B: Neck circumference within normal limits
options.C: BMI greater than 35 and observed apnea episodes

trapLogic: Recognizing STOP-BANG risk factors (snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, pressure/BP, BMI>35, age>50, neck size, male gender) versus normal/negative findings is the core skill tested.

text: What item must ALWAYS be kept at the bedside of a client with a new tracheostomy?

options.B: A spare tracheostomy tube (same size) and obturator

trapLogic: Trap: distractors are plausible respiratory equipment, but the specific, testable safety rule is the spare same-size trach tube + obturator for emergency reinsertion.

text: When suctioning a tracheostomy, which technique is correct?

options.A: Apply suction while inserting the catheter
options.B: Insert without suction, apply suction only on withdrawal, for a maximum of 10 seconds
options.C: Suction continuously for up to 30 seconds for a thorough clean
options.D: Suction only once every 8 hours regardless of secretions

trapLogic: Sequencing + time-limit trap: suction is applied on withdrawal only, capped at 10 seconds, to prevent hypoxia and mucosal trauma.

text: When should a tracheostomy cuff be inflated?

options.B: Never — cuffs should always remain deflated
options.C: During meals and while on mechanical ventilation

trapLogic: Cuff-timing trap: inflated during feeding/ventilation to protect the airway and prevent aspiration; deflated at other times per protocol to reduce tracheal injury risk.

text: A client reports hoarseness that has persisted for 3 weeks. What should the nurse prioritize?

options.A: Reassure the client this is likely a common cold and will resolve
options.B: Recognize this as a red flag requiring further evaluation for laryngeal cancer
options.C: Recommend voice rest only, no referral needed

trapLogic: Trap: hoarseness >2 weeks is explicitly a red-flag symptom for laryngeal cancer, not something to attribute to a cold — the exact duration cutoff is testable.

text: A client had a total laryngectomy. Which action is CONTRAINDICATED?

options.B: Placing a standard non-rebreather mask over the nose and mouth for oxygen
options.C: Using a stoma mask for oxygen delivery

trapLogic: Core anatomy trap: after laryngectomy, the airway is ONLY through the stoma — an NRB mask over nose/mouth would deliver no oxygen at all and must never be used.

text: Which position best reduces aspiration risk in a client receiving tube feedings?

options.B: HOB elevated 30-45 degrees

trapLogic: Standard aspiration-precaution recall — HOB 30-45° during and after feeds is the tested safety measure, versus flat/supine positioning which increases risk.

text: A client with an altered LOC who has been lying supine develops a fever and productive cough. A chest X-ray shows an infiltrate. Which lobe is MOST likely involved?

options.B: Right lower lobe (RLL)

trapLogic: Gravity-dependent trap: in a supine patient, aspirated material most commonly settles in the right lower lobe due to the anatomy of the right mainstem bronchus.

text: A client develops pneumonia symptoms 5 days after hospital admission for an unrelated surgery. How is this classified?

options.B: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) — onset after 48 hours of admission
options.D: Aspiration pneumonia only, regardless of timing

trapLogic: Definition/timing trap: HAP is defined by onset AFTER 48 hours of hospitalization; a symptom onset at day 5 clearly fits HAP, not CAP.

text: Which lung cancer type is most strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes and is considered the most aggressive?

options.B: Squamous cell carcinoma

trapLogic: Subtype trap: NSCLC subtypes (adeno, squamous, large cell) are grouped together, but SCLC stands apart as the most aggressive with strong paraneoplastic association.

text: A client has a productive cough for 4 months this year and had a similar pattern last year as well. This history is consistent with which component of COPD?

options.B: Chronic bronchitis (productive cough ≥3 months/year for ≥2 consecutive years)

trapLogic: Exact-duration definitional trap: chronic bronchitis requires a productive cough for 3+ months per year for 2+ consecutive years — a 'close but not quite' duration is a common distractor.

text: What is the key feature that distinguishes asthma from COPD?

options.A: Asthma airway obstruction is largely REVERSIBLE; COPD obstruction is largely irreversible
options.B: Asthma only affects children
options.C: COPD is always reversible with bronchodilators
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two

trapLogic: Core pathophysiology trap tested repeatedly: reversibility is the defining distinction, not age group or medication response alone.

text: A client using a dry powder inhaler (DPI) needs to inhale:

options.A: Slowly, over several seconds, like an MDI
options.B: Quickly and forcefully to activate and disperse the powder
options.C: Not at all — DPIs are exhaled into
options.D: Only during an acute asthma attack

trapLogic: Technique-reversal trap: MDIs require a SLOW inhalation; DPIs require a FAST, forceful inhalation — the opposite technique. DPIs are also not recommended during acute attacks since the client often can't generate enough inspiratory force.

text: Which diagnostic result confirms a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis, and when should pancreatic enzyme replacement be taken?

options.A: Sweat chloride <30 mEq/L; enzymes taken once daily at bedtime
options.B: Sweat chloride >60 mEq/L; enzymes taken with ALL meals and snacks
options.C: Sweat chloride is not used for diagnosis; enzymes taken only with breakfast
options.D: A normal sweat chloride test with enzymes taken on an empty stomach

trapLogic: Two-part recall trap: know both the diagnostic cutoff (sweat chloride >60 mEq/L) AND the practical teaching point (enzymes must go with every meal/snack, not just once daily).
